EMS Red Zones

By: Catherine Rice | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Paramedics are under siege in some parts of Cape Town, disrupting health services to those who desperately need it.

Unique Selling Point:
There are eleven Red Zones in the Western Cape. Paramedics cannot enter these areas without a police escort as crime is rife, impacting critical health service delivery. The number of violent attacks on paramedics has been rising at an alarming rate, resulting in absenteeism and work-related illnesses. In 2023, 43 attacks were recorded.

Summary:
There have been 43 attacks on Emergency Medical Services staff in Cape Town in the past year, ranging from robbery, hijacking and stoning to physical assault and damage to property. The risk for workplace violence is exceptionally high as they work in communities where crime is rife. In the Western Cape, there are eleven red zones. Paramedics cannot enter these zones unless they are accompanied by police. In this insert, we join paramedics on a public holiday at night to experience their work conditions firsthand. The job is a calling for Rudowaan Fredericks and Vuyisinani Oyo. They must be vigilante at all times while they work. For Rudowaan, music is what helps him de-stress and when at home he plays his trombone to relax. Classical music gets him through gruelling twelve hour shifts and he often plays it en route to medical emergencies. We also speak to Victor Labuschagne who has been a paramedic for over twenty years and has been attacked in red zones twice, despite having police escorts during both incidents.

Script:


VO 1 Late night revelry in one of Cape Town’s most crime-ridden areas, a regular destination for paramedics on night shift.

VO 2 Alcohol and drugs fuel an atmosphere that can turn at any moment, making this place - and others like it - hostile terrain for people simply trying to do their jobs.

VO 2a Called upon to save lives in one of the most violent and unpredictable places in the country, they work under the watchful eye of the police.

VO 2b This is a red zone.

CUT TO BLACK

VO 3 It’s just before Christmas, the height of Cape Town’s tourist season, notoriously busy for its emergency services.

VO 4 As day turns to night, paramedics at one of the city’s medical emergency centres, prepare to go on shift.

VO 5 They’ll see a side to Cape Town many visiting the city couldn’t possibly imagine. An environment in which their dedication to those in need doesn’t spare them the attention of violent criminals.

LINK ERIN Day 1/Clip 7609 When it comes to saving lives, no area is off limits for emergency services, not even the City’s red zones. The paramedics presence on the frontlines over the festive season is more important than ever.

VO 6 There are eleven so-called red zones around Cape Town. Their exact locations aren’t publicised, but they’re deemed too dangerous for paramedics to operate in without additional support. That means going in with a police escort - a frustrating process that often slows them down.

NATSOUND Clip 7617/ Hugging each other “We have a long night ahead of us. You ready?”

VO 7 We’re joining paramedics Rudowaan Fredericks and Vuyisanani Oyo in Ambulance 116.

VO 8 Within minutes they get a priority one callout - a sixteen year old boy has been shot in the leg. (PAUSE) He lives in a red zone…

VO 8a En route, they will have to make a crucial stop.

NATSOUND Clip 7649 Day 1 Greg / Radio call for police escort / Clip 7656 “Ambulance 116 at Blue Downs Saps)

VO 9 It’s an obvious emergency, but the stop over at a police station to arrange backup eats away at the time. It’s laborious and frustrating but a sign of just how seriously the emergency services view the red zones and how conditions within them have deteriorated.

UPSOUND Rudowaan Fredericks (clip 7937) Time code 12:58You have the information in front of you. You know what’s happening at that address but you can’t do anything. You are trained, you have all the resources to save somebody’s life but because you have to get a police escort and waiting periods, its sometimes too late when we get there

LINK ERIN clip 7663/ Day 1 (Greg) Fortunately, this time its taken a matter of seconds, but we’re told it can sometimes take up to three hours to get back up.

VO 10 In the growing darkness of this volatile area, the paramedics navigate the streets in search of their patient.

NATSOUND Day 1 / Greg cam / Clip 7669 Rudowaan: we are entering a red zone now”

NATSOUND Clip 7674 Time code 00:46 Vuyisanani asks is it no 5…community member says neighbour took him to hospital in private transport. Time code 00:50“We apologise for taking so long, because we have to via police for safety issues.

VO 11 When patients are taken to hospital in a private vehicle, paramedics are often only informed after arriving at the scene..

NATSOUND Clip 7674 Time code 01:48. Going to stand down”.

VO 12 Working in these conditions takes a toll. Between call outs, music provides Rudowaan a much-needed outlet, a moment to forget the chaos that surrounds him.

UPSOUND Rudowaan Time code 11:22 It gives that atmosphere of tranquility at the workplace, in the office or in the ambulance or response vehicle”.

VO 13 But, these moments are all too brief, as the ambulance radio shatters whatever tranquility he’s able to find. Western Cape Emergency Medical Services respond to about 750 000 calls a year. Over the festive season alone, they receive around 65 000.

NATSOUND Radio callouts

VO 14 Many of their patients are victims of violent crime in the notorious red zones.

UPSOUND Vuyisinani Oyo (Clip 7839 Time code: 00:19) The red zone at times becomes a no go area because sometimes the red zones get so volatile that even SAPS can’t escort us.

VO15 When they do make it in, they need to be vigilant at all times.

UPSOUND Vuyisanani Oyo “Clip 7838 Time code 03:04 Its just not easy when you’re in those areas. Its not easy at all. Time code: 03:28 Especially when its dark and it’s loadshedding, its more dangerous.

VO 16 It's not long before there’s another call out… to another red zone.

NATSOUND Rudowaan Clip 7745 Time code: 00:35 Law enforcement is available to escort. We will take first person. Remember there is someone stabbed in the neck.”

VO 17 The stab wound needs stitches, but the patient refuses to be taken to hospital.

UPSOUND Rudowaan Clip 7756 / Day 1/ 00:49 Patient refused transport, standing down. (00:58 use these visuals slow down. Let it breathe)

UPSOUND Vuyisanani Clip 7759 Time code 01:50 We felt like anything can happen any time. Because they all drunk. 02:25 Luckily today, there’s no shooting.

PAUSE (allow the piece to slow down as per John’s notes..)

UPSOUND Victor Labuschagne (Clip 7808 Time code 1:15 Unfortunately with the job comes danger. In the last couple of years its picked up.

VO 18 (Cam 2 / his face in mirror driving response vehicle C5057 around there) Victor Labuschagne has been a paramedic for 26 years and has seen it all -

NATSOUND Day 1 / Cam 1 Clip 7870 Victor “Is it just assault?”

VO 15 Despite having a police escort, he’s been attacked in red zones twice.

UPSOUND Victor Labuschagne Clip 7810 Time code: 02:45 As I approached a stop street, I saw one guy passing the ambulance. We don’t know why - he fired at the ambulance so I got shot. Time code: 03:24 I was hit in my chest, fractured two ribs, I was bruised. And then on the other incident a guy stabbed me on the back. Luckily, I’m still here (laughs)

VO 16 Victor made a full physical recovery after the attacks, but they took a mental toll.

UPSOUND Victor Labuschangne Clip 7809 Time code 07:37 After the whole shooting incident, I was off for quite a bit. But, I just felt I needed to get back into the area. I needed to face my demons again.

VO 17 Not all paramedics are able to bounce back. In 2023 alone, there were over 40 attacks on paramedics in the Western Cape, often leaving them with post traumatic stress - or PTSD..

UPSOUND Craig Wylie / W Cape EMS Director Clip 7914 / Day 2 Time code: 32:10 In terms of absenteeism, it’s a huge problem, it is anything from anxiety to PTSD and anything from a couple of days off to years that the practitioners are not able to come back to work.

VO 18 The Province’s Director of Emergency Medical Services, Craig Wylie, says the safety of paramedics is essential. That’s why permanent red zones were declared in the province in 2016.

UPSOUND Craig Wylie / Cam 1 / Day 2 / Clip 7915 We’ll always go, but the response may be delayed” Time code: 08:17 “If an area does become volatile, we’ll declare that as a temporary red zone which means watch out for a short time”

ERIN Clip 7914 02:12 From what I understand there are some areas where even the police are afraid to go.

UPSOUND Craig Wylie Clip 7914 Time code: 02:20 That’s not always the case, but there are cases of unrest like we saw in recent taxi violence where an ambulance was actually burnt on the N2. Where the police aren’t happy to go into area called No go zones (whatsapped visuals of burnt out ambulance)

VO 19 Danger lurks on almost every call out. Sometimes, the biggest threat comes from communities frustrated by the long waits - a vicious circle.

UPSOUND Victor Labuschagne Time code: 08:34 People in green or any ambulance service, we’re there to help. We’re not there for anything else. If it’s your mother, your baby, your brother, and you have to wait for an ambulance for three hours because we had to go to a police station, its not our fault.

VO 20 And yet, despite the challenges and almost constant threat to their safety, for the paramedics this is a calling.

UPSOUND Vuyisanani Oso Clip 7839 00:49 I love this job. There’s not a single day, I say I don’t want to be at work. I always want to be out there and help people.

NATSOUND

VO 21 A priority call comes through - it’s urgent, time to move..

VO 22 (Clip 7851 / Day 1 / Cam 1 driving into area onwards) Police are already on the scene for this case, so Rudowaan and Vuyisanani can head straight there..

VO 23 A man has been viciously assaulted and is in a critical condition..

LINK Clip 7882 Time code: 00:37 From what we understand the patient being treated right now was assaulted a little further down the road. There are pools of blood here and you can see the drag marks leading to the car where currently he’s fighting for his life. (also clip 7879 Greg gets shot of blood marks from where his body was dragged)

NATSOUND Woman sobbing Clip 7866 Time code:00:55

VO 24 The man was left for dead in the middle of the street - he has a collapsed lung, multiple lacerations, and a possible brain injury.

VO 25 The paramedics perform a chest decompression, a life saving procedure.

NATSOUND paramedic asking woman to contact patient’s relatives

VO 26 Rudowaan says a lot has changed for emergency services staff in recent years.

UPSOUND Rudowaan (run audio under visuals please) clip 7938 The answer is in the community. Community leaders they have to address this, the elements within the community, Time code 26:36 There really is people in the community that suffers, that must pay the ultimate price because of elements that live in the next street”

VO 27 It’s a sad reality that would discourage people less committed to their cause. And in the moments when that reality gets too much, Rudowaan has his music.

UPSOUND Rudowaan (play audio under visuals) Time code 04:16 When I come home after a difficult shift, I immerse myself with music. Music is a universal language. Music brings out emotions you can’t even say in words.

VO 27 When his shift is over, Rudowaan often plays his trombone.

VO 28 The images of the night before fading away. (maybe slowmo of Rudowaan performing life saving care to assault patient)

VO 29 The sun rising signals the end of the team’s twelve hour shift. New teams will take over for the daylight hours with 140 ambulances on call across the province. (play out with Rudowaan’s music under visuals)

We also speak to Victor Labuschagne who has been a paramedic for over twenty years and has been attacked in red zones twice, despite having police escorts during both incidents.
